items.question:
A data analyst at a retail company builds a few-shot prompt to classify customer feedback into five sentiment categories. She starts with exactly one example per category (five examples total). Classification quality is inconsistent — especially for ambiguous feedback that blends categories. A colleague suggests simply doubling or tripling the example count across the board.

What is the MOST accurate guidance about scaling few-shot example counts?

options.A: Adding examples beyond five offers no benefit because Claude's parametric knowledge already covers common sentiment tasks.
options.B: Example count should always match the number of output categories — five categories require exactly five examples.
options.C: More examples help when existing examples are ambiguous or when the task has high input variation; returns diminish as examples become redundant.
options.D: Doubling examples always improves accuracy proportionally, so the analyst should aim for at least ten examples per category.

items.question:
A procurement specialist at a government agency embeds a supplier evaluation rubric and a 30-page supplier proposal in the same prompt. Claude's feedback mixes rubric language with analysis of the proposal, making it difficult to distinguish evaluation criteria from findings.

What is the MOST effective structural change to prevent this confusion?

options.A: Send the rubric and the proposal in two separate conversations.
options.B: Wrap the rubric in `<rubric>...</rubric>` tags and the proposal in `<proposal>...</proposal>` tags to separate instructions from content.
options.C: Ask Claude to summarise the rubric at the top of each response before providing feedback.
options.D: Use numbered headings to label each section of the combined prompt.

items.question:
A marketing analyst at a telecoms company sends a single Claude prompt requesting: (1) a summary of last quarter's campaign performance, (2) budget reallocation recommendations, (3) two draft social media posts for Q3, and (4) a French translation of those posts.

What design principle does this prompt MOST clearly violate?

options.A: Prompts should not include translation tasks alongside analytical tasks.
options.B: Marketing prompts must comply with brand and tone guidelines before submission.
options.C: Campaign analysis requires a dedicated model tier and cannot be mixed with creative writing.
options.D: Each prompt should be scoped to one clear job so that outputs can be reviewed and refined independently.

items.question:
An actuarial analyst at a mid-size insurer wants Claude to calculate premium adjustments, draft policyholder notifications, and prepare a regulator summary — all from the same dataset. A colleague recommends breaking the work into three separate prompts. The analyst worries this will add unnecessary complexity.

Which is the MOST significant benefit of task decomposition that the colleague is likely pointing to?

options.A: Each stage's output can be reviewed and corrected before it becomes the input to the next stage, preventing errors from compounding.
options.B: Separate prompts prevent context-window overload that would otherwise cause the combined prompt to be truncated.
options.C: Claude produces shorter responses when each prompt is narrowly scoped, which reduces API latency.
options.D: Decomposed tasks can be automatically routed to the optimal model tier based on task complexity.

items.question:
A content strategist at a media company uses a three-stage workflow. Stage 1: Claude outlines a 10-article editorial series. Stage 2: Claude drafts Article 1 using the approved outline. Stage 3: Claude revises Article 1 based on editor feedback.

The strategist has completed Stage 1 and received an outline that includes an unexpected structural angle the editor has approved. She is now ready to begin Stage 2.

What should the strategist do NEXT?

options.A: Start a new chat session for Stage 2 so Claude begins without any Stage 1 context.
options.B: Ask Claude to produce a condensed one-paragraph version of the outline before drafting.
options.C: Paste the approved Stage 1 outline directly into the Stage 2 prompt so Claude drafts from the actual approved content.
options.D: Tell Claude the article count and topic names without including the full outline text.

items.question:
A financial analyst at a private equity fund asks Claude to assess the creditworthiness of a prospective portfolio company. The first response is confident in tone but shows no intermediate reasoning — just a conclusion. The analyst must be able to explain and defend the assessment in an investment committee meeting. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO prompt adjustments are MOST likely to make the assessment reviewable and defensible?

options.A: Ask Claude to list each factor it is weighing — liquidity, leverage, coverage, market position — before stating an overall conclusion.
options.B: Restrict Claude to using only information from the uploaded financial statements.
options.C: Specify that the output must be formatted in a table with coloured cells for risk levels.
options.D: Ask Claude to produce a separate assessment for each dimension — liquidity, leverage, coverage — before synthesising a final view.
options.E: Switch to the highest-tier model to improve the depth of reasoning.

items.question:
A policy analyst at a federal agency uploads a 90-page environmental impact assessment and asks: "What does this document say about groundwater contamination?" The response is superficial and misses details from a subsection near the document's midpoint.

What prompt adjustment is MOST likely to improve the completeness of future responses?

options.A: Upload the document as a plain-text file instead of a PDF to make the content more parseable.
options.B: Enable Research mode to allow Claude to cross-reference external databases on groundwater standards.
options.C: Ask Claude to produce a full executive summary of the document before answering the specific question.
options.D: Place the specific question after the document text and instruct Claude to cite section headings when referencing content.

items.question:
A compliance officer at a multinational bank deploys a few-shot prompt to classify customer complaints into Routine, Escalated, and Regulatory tiers. All training examples were drawn from complaints submitted in one region. After global rollout, the prompt consistently misclassifies formal legal-register complaints common in other jurisdictions.

What is the MOST precise diagnosis of this failure?

options.A: The model cannot process complaints written in a formal legal register without jurisdiction-specific fine-tuning.
options.B: A three-tier classification is too coarse for a global complaint taxonomy and should be expanded.
options.C: The training examples lacked sufficient variation in tone, register, and jurisdictional vocabulary to generalise across the full complaint population.
options.D: Few-shot examples embedded in a chat prompt are overridden by fine-tuning data, which was not provided for the global population.

items.question:
A technical writer at a logistics company embeds a lengthy API specification inside a prompt, then appends editing instructions below it. Claude's edits repeatedly revise sections of the specification itself rather than following the editing instructions appended after it.

What is the SIMPLEST structural fix?

options.A: Wrap the specification in `<document>...</document>` tags and the instructions in `<instructions>...</instructions>` tags.
options.B: Move the API specification into a Project knowledge document and reference it by name in the prompt.
options.C: Shorten the specification to only the sections Claude needs to reference for the current task.
options.D: Send the specification and the editing instructions in separate messages so Claude sees them sequentially.

items.question:
A recruitment coordinator at a staffing agency builds a five-example few-shot prompt to help Claude screen CVs. Four examples show clear-hire decisions; one shows a borderline case. In testing, Claude labels borderline CVs as clear-hire more often than expected.

What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: Five examples exceed the optimal count for binary screening tasks, causing the model to average across them.
options.B: The skewed distribution of examples — four clear-hire to one borderline — biases Claude toward the majority outcome when inputs are ambiguous.
options.C: Claude cannot reliably distinguish borderline from clear-hire cases without an explicit numerical scoring rubric.
options.D: The borderline example should have been omitted because it introduces conflicting signal.

items.question:
A learning and development manager at a 90,000-person energy company is building a workflow where Claude evaluates written development submissions from 200 employees and generates personalised feedback letters. She asks a consultant whether a single complex prompt or a decomposed two-stage pipeline would be more appropriate. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO advantages of a decomposed pipeline are MOST relevant to this use case?

options.A: Decomposition automatically routes the evaluation stage to a more powerful model tier than the drafting stage.
options.B: A human reviewer can check all evaluations before any feedback letters are generated, preventing flawed evaluations from propagating into letters that reach employees.
options.C: Separate prompts consume fewer total tokens than a single combined prompt.
options.D: Separating evaluation from drafting makes it straightforward to adjust the criteria or letter template independently when quality issues arise.
options.E: Claude can process multi-stage workflows only when each stage is submitted as a separate API call.

items.question:
A procurement manager uses Claude daily for routine supplier emails. The emails are well-structured and match her preferred tone without any examples in the prompt. After reading about few-shot prompting, she adds three example emails to every prompt.

What is the MOST likely outcome of this change?

options.A: The examples add prompt length and latency with no noticeable quality improvement because zero-shot output already meets the standard.
options.B: Output quality improves proportionally to the three examples added.
options.C: Claude ignores the examples and continues generating from its training data alone.
options.D: Adding examples to an already-working prompt introduces inconsistency as Claude tries to reconcile the examples with its instructions.

items.question:
A compliance analyst uses labelled prose headings — "SECTION 1 — POLICY TEXT" and "SECTION 2 — INSTRUCTIONS" — to separate sections of a long prompt. Claude's responses sometimes blend policy language into what should be purely an instructions-driven output. A colleague suggests replacing the prose headings with XML-style tags.

What is the PRIMARY advantage of XML tags over labelled prose headings?

options.A: XML tags render as formatted boxes in Claude's UI, making it visually clearer which section is active.
options.B: XML tags provide explicit, machine-readable semantic boundaries that Claude is specifically trained to recognise as structural delimiters.
options.C: XML tags allow multiple documents to be submitted in a single prompt where prose headings allow only one.
options.D: XML tags automatically validate the document's structure before Claude processes the prompt.

items.question:
A data scientist at a biotech firm uses two techniques. Sometimes she breaks a large analysis into three separate, independent Claude prompts. Other times she uses a conversation where each message explicitly passes the previous output forward. Her manager asks her to articulate the difference between task decomposition and prompt chaining.

Which description MOST accurately distinguishes the two?

options.A: Task decomposition and prompt chaining are synonymous — both describe breaking work into sequential Claude turns.
options.B: Task decomposition is for API-based workflows; prompt chaining is for interactive chat sessions.
options.C: Task decomposition breaks a complex job into discrete stages with individually reviewable outputs; prompt chaining passes the output of one stage as the explicit input to the next.
options.D: Prompt chaining is for creative tasks; task decomposition is for analytical or data tasks.

items.question:
A research analyst asks Claude to produce a competitive landscape report with a dedicated section for each of five competitors. The response comes back as continuous prose with no section structure. A junior colleague recommends adding "think step by step" to fix the formatting issue.

What is the CORRECT diagnosis and recommended fix?

options.A: The colleague is correct — chain-of-thought will cause Claude to reason through each competitor separately, which produces the desired section structure.
options.B: The model needs more background on each competitor to produce distinct sections.
options.C: Chain-of-thought was missing from the original prompt and must be added before any formatting instructions.
options.D: The formatting problem is unrelated to reasoning; the fix is to explicitly specify the required section headings and output structure in the prompt.

items.question:
A technical writer at a software company wants Claude to produce API documentation in the firm's specific house style. She is deciding between writing detailed prose instructions describing the style or supplying three completed documentation pages as examples. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO conditions MOST favour using examples over prose instructions?

options.A: The house style involves idiomatic phrasing and structural conventions that are difficult to describe precisely in words.
options.B: The documentation pages will each exceed 2,000 words.
options.C: Previous attempts using only prose instructions have consistently missed key stylistic elements.
options.D: The technical writer personally finds examples easier to prepare than prose descriptions.
options.E: The API has more than fifteen endpoints to document.

items.question:
A legal analyst adds ten few-shot examples to a contract-clause classification prompt. Output quality remains inconsistent for clauses classified as "unusual." Investigation reveals all ten examples show standard or non-standard clauses, with no example of an unusual clause.

What does this situation MOST clearly illustrate?

options.A: Ten examples exceed the practical limit for few-shot prompting, creating noise in the classification signal.
options.B: Example representativeness across all output categories matters more than total example count.
options.C: The classification task is too complex for few-shot prompting and requires fine-tuning on the firm's contract corpus.
options.D: Claude requires an equal number of examples for each class; the unusual class needs exactly ten examples to match the others.

items.question:
A financial controller designs a three-stage pipeline: Stage 1 generates a 12-month cash flow projection; Stage 2 identifies months where cash falls below a reserve threshold; Stage 3 drafts mitigation actions for each flagged month. She considers running each stage fully independently (starting from scratch with the original data) versus chaining them (each stage receives the previous stage's output).

What design decision is MOST correct?

options.A: Fully independent prompts are always preferable because they prevent context contamination between stages.
options.B: All three stages should be combined in a single prompt for coherence and efficiency.
options.C: A prompt chain is appropriate here because Stage 2 and Stage 3 are computationally dependent on upstream output — Stage 3 can only draft mitigations for months that Stage 2 has flagged.
options.D: All three stages should be treated as independent because they share the same source dataset.

items.question:
An HR analyst learns about using XML-style tags in prompts. She asks whether she needs valid XML syntax — proper attribute declarations, schema conformance, namespace prefixes — or whether simple descriptive labels like `<policy>` and `</policy>` are sufficient.

What is the CORRECT guidance?

options.A: Claude requires well-formed XML with proper attribute declarations; otherwise it will misparse the tag structure.
options.B: Only tag names from the Claude documentation are recognised; custom names like `<policy>` are ignored.
options.C: Tags must be nested according to XML hierarchy rules or Claude will treat enclosed content as unparsed text.
options.D: Simple, descriptive tag names are sufficient; Claude uses them as semantic markers and does not require XML conformance.

items.question:
An insurance adjuster needs Claude to extract all coverage exclusions from a 60-page policy document. A colleague proposes two approaches: (a) ask Claude to summarise the document, then extract exclusions from the summary; or (b) ask Claude to scan each section and list any exclusions found, then compile a final list.

Which approach is MORE reliable for complete extraction, and why?

options.A: Approach (b) is more reliable because systematic section-level scanning reduces the risk that exclusions in less prominent sections are lost during a summary step.
options.B: Approach (a) is more reliable because a summary removes irrelevant content and concentrates Claude's attention on key provisions.
options.C: Both approaches are equally reliable; the choice is purely a formatting preference.
options.D: Approach (a) is more reliable because summaries are more token-efficient, reducing context pressure.

items.question:
A communications director writes a prompt asking Claude to review a 25-page media brief and suggest three headline angles. She places her three instructions at the top of the prompt, then the brief below. A content consultant recommends reversing the order — brief first, instructions second.

What is the PRIMARY reason for placing the document before the instructions?

options.A: Claude tokenises long text more efficiently when documents precede instructions.
options.B: Placing the document before the instructions ensures Claude processes the full content before the task is specified, reducing early pattern-matching that stops thorough reading.
options.C: Instructions placed before long documents are dropped from Claude's active context by the time it reaches the document text.
options.D: The document must precede the task so Claude aligns its response to the document's section order rather than the instruction order.

items.question:
A strategy consultant has completed Turn 1 of a two-stage workflow: Claude analysed a 40-slide competitor presentation and produced a list of 12 strategic themes. The consultant reviewed the list, removed two themes outside the client's scope, and now has an approved 10-theme list. She is preparing to submit Turn 2, which will draft a narrative briefing based on the approved themes.

What should the consultant do NEXT?

options.A: Start a new conversation so Claude generates the briefing without influence from the competitor deck.
options.B: Ask Claude to consolidate the 10 themes into three broader clusters before drafting the briefing.
options.C: Include the approved 10-theme list explicitly in the Turn 2 prompt, labelled as the approved input for the briefing.
options.D: Re-paste the full 40-slide competitor deck content into Turn 2 so Claude has complete source context.

items.question:
A QA manager at a pharmaceutical manufacturer wants Claude to review 50 batch records for GMP compliance and classify each as Compliant, Minor Deviation, or Major Deviation, then produce a summary report for the site director. Initial tests show inconsistent classification across all three tiers and a generic, non-specific summary. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO changes MOST directly address both problems?

options.A: Add one or two representative examples for each deviation tier to anchor the classification criteria concretely.
options.B: Switch to the highest-tier model to improve classification precision and summary depth.
options.C: Ask Claude to generate the summary first and use it to inform the per-record classifications.
options.D: Decompose the workflow so classification and summary drafting are separate prompts, with human review of all classifications before the summary is generated.
options.E: Wrap each batch record in `<record>` tags to help Claude process them individually.

items.question:
A copywriter at a retail brand needs Claude to produce product descriptions that are consistently upbeat, second-person, and under 60 words. She is deciding whether to provide example descriptions or whether clear prose instructions would be sufficient.

What is the MOST accurate guidance for this decision?

options.A: Examples are always more reliable than prose for tone-setting tasks in marketing contexts.
options.B: Prose instructions cannot specify tone accurately — examples are the only reliable mechanism for tone calibration.
options.C: Both approaches produce identical results; the choice is purely a matter of personal workflow preference.
options.D: For simple, clearly describable constraints such as person, tone, and word count, precise prose instructions are often sufficient and add less prompt overhead than examples.

items.question:
A UX researcher wants Claude to produce user interview summaries using an internal empathy-mapping format. The format has subtle conventions — placement of direct quotes vs. paraphrases, theme labelling style — that emerged informally over years of practice and have never been fully documented. Prose instructions have produced drafts that miss the nuances.

What prompting approach is MOST likely to produce output that matches the internal format?

options.A: Provide two or three completed empathy-map summaries as examples, letting Claude infer the conventions directly from demonstrated practice.
options.B: Write a detailed specification document describing every convention and upload it as a supporting file.
options.C: Switch to a more capable model tier, which will handle subtle formatting conventions more reliably.
options.D: Ask Claude to draft freely and then iteratively correct it through multiple follow-up messages until it matches the desired format.

items.question:
An operations manager asks Claude to produce a weekly project status report in a table with four columns: Project, Status, Owner, Next Action. The response comes back as bullet-point prose with no table.

What is the CORRECT fix?

options.A: Add "think step by step" to the prompt so Claude reasons through each project before formatting.
options.B: Ask Claude to reason through the project list before presenting the table so the format emerges from the analysis.
options.C: Explicitly specify the table format in the prompt, naming the four required columns.
options.D: Provide an example table from a previous week so Claude can match the structure.

items.question:
An M&A analyst designs a workflow: Stage 1 extracts financial data from a target company filing; Stage 2 applies three valuation methods to produce a range; Stage 3 drafts the valuation section of a client investment memo. The analyst is deciding whether to combine Stages 2 and 3 into a single prompt or keep them separate.

What is the STRONGEST argument for keeping Stages 2 and 3 as separate prompts?

options.A: The numerical outputs of Stage 2 require human review before they appear in a client-facing document in Stage 3 — separation creates a mandatory accuracy checkpoint.
options.B: Stage 2 must use a different model tier than Stage 3 because valuation requires more reasoning depth than memo drafting.
options.C: Combining numerical and narrative tasks in a single prompt causes Claude to misround financial figures.
options.D: The structured output format of Stage 2 is incompatible with the narrative output format of Stage 3 when combined.

items.question:
A content manager is clarifying the difference between multi-turn conversation and prompt chaining. In multi-turn conversation she asks follow-up questions in the same chat. In prompt chaining she explicitly captures, reviews, and pastes a prior output into the next prompt.

What is the KEY distinction between the two?

options.A: Multi-turn conversation is used only for creative work; prompt chaining is used only for analytical workflows.
options.B: Prompt chaining requires API access; multi-turn conversation is only available in the chat interface.
options.C: In a multi-turn conversation, Claude retains all messages automatically; in prompt chaining, only the explicitly selected and verified prior output is passed forward.
options.D: Multi-turn relies on passive context accumulation within a session; prompt chaining is an active design pattern where the practitioner controls exactly which verified output is embedded as structured input to the next stage.

items.question:
A bid manager embeds a 60-page RFP document and a set of evaluation criteria in a single prompt. Instructions are placed before the document. Claude's response addresses only the first five evaluation criteria and ignores the remaining twelve. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO structural changes MOST directly address this failure?

options.A: Wrap the evaluation criteria in `<criteria>...</criteria>` tags to explicitly separate them from the RFP document content.
options.B: Move the evaluation criteria and instructions to the end of the prompt, after the RFP document.
options.C: Reduce the RFP to a two-page executive summary before submitting.
options.D: Ask Claude to confirm it has read all seventeen evaluation criteria before beginning the analysis.
options.E: Change the response format to bullet points to make it easier to verify coverage.

items.question:
A legal analyst is reviewing 15 contracts for a specific clause type. She is choosing between (a) submitting all 15 contracts in one very long prompt, or (b) a prompt chain with one contract per turn, passing a running list of findings forward. A partner argues approach (a) is simpler. The analyst prefers (b) but cannot articulate the advantage precisely.

What is the MOST accurate articulation of approach (b)'s advantage?

options.A: Approach (b) reduces total token consumption across the full review.
options.B: Approach (b) creates per-contract quality checkpoints, allowing the analyst to verify each contract's findings before they contribute to the cumulative list used in the final recommendation.
options.C: Approach (a) risks exceeding the context window, making approach (b) the only technically feasible option.
options.D: Approach (b) is preferred because Claude's quality degrades materially when presented with very long contexts.

items.question:
A strategy director asks Claude to evaluate whether to acquire a competitor. The response is three sentences with a clear recommendation but no visible reasoning. The director must present a defensible analysis to a board meeting. (Choose TWO)

Which TWO prompt adjustments MOST improve the analytical rigour of the output?

options.A: Restrict Claude to using only data from the uploaded financial model and ignore its general market knowledge.
options.B: Request that the output be formatted as a formal board memorandum with an executive summary section.
options.C: Instruct Claude to reason through each evaluation dimension — strategic fit, financial impact, integration risk, competitive response — before stating an overall recommendation.
options.D: Ask Claude to produce a separate analytical memo for each dimension before synthesising a final view in a concluding prompt.
options.E: Switch to the highest-tier model to improve the depth of the reasoning produced.

items.question:
A software ops analyst at a 400-person logistics firm asks Claude to extract delivery status records from a batch of 80 emails and output the results. Claude returns a prose summary paragraph instead of structured data. The analyst needs system-importable output.

What is the MOST direct fix for the next run?

options.A: Add an explicit format instruction: "Output a JSON array, one object per email, with fields: sender, delivery_status, and eta."
options.B: Switch from Sonnet to Opus, which defaults to structured output for data extraction tasks.
options.C: Ask Claude to re-read its prose response and convert it to JSON in a follow-up turn.
options.D: Break the task into two prompts — one for extraction and one for formatting.

items.question:
A content strategist at a media company sends Claude a draft article with the prompt: "Do not use passive voice, do not include jargon, do not exceed 600 words, and don't repeat yourself." The revision still contains passive constructions and runs to 680 words.

What is the MOST likely cause of this outcome?

options.A: Claude cannot process more than two negative constraints simultaneously in a single prompt.
options.B: Stacking multiple negative constraints distributes attention across prohibitions, making each one less reliably enforced than an equivalent positive instruction would be.
options.C: Passive voice detection is a grammar feature that applies only when Claude is in a code-editing context.
options.D: 600 words fell below Claude's default compression threshold, so the length limit was ignored.

items.question:
A grant writer at a non-profit prepares a 2-page project brief for a foundation application. She prompts Claude: "Write a detailed overview of our water access programme." Claude returns a 1,200-word response with extensive historical background. She needs approximately 400 words.

Which prompt change would MOST reliably produce the intended output?

options.A: "Keep this concise."
options.B: "Write a short response."
options.C: "Write approximately 400 words. Cover: programme goals, target population, and measurable outcomes. Exclude historical background."
options.D: "Summarise in bullet points only."

items.question:
A RevOps lead drafts a single prompt asking Claude to: analyse six months of pipeline data, identify stalled deals, draft personalised follow-up emails for each rep, summarise recommended next steps, and create a slide outline for the upcoming QBR. Claude returns a response that touches each task but is shallow on all of them.

Which anti-pattern MOST explains this outcome?

options.A: The prompt used informal language, causing Claude to deprioritise the analytical tasks.
options.B: The pipeline data was too large for Claude to process accurately in a single context window.
options.C: Claude applies a per-task token budget when multiple tasks are bundled, capping depth on each.
options.D: The prompt bundled five distinct tasks with different output types and success criteria into one request, preventing deep execution on any single task.

items.question:
A procurement specialist needs to compare seven vendors across four criteria: price, delivery lead time, warranty terms, and compliance rating. She will use the comparison in a stakeholder presentation built in a documentation tool that renders markdown.

Which output format should she specify in her prompt?

options.A: A markdown table with vendors as rows and criteria as columns, so it renders directly in the documentation tool.
options.B: A numbered list of vendors, with each vendor's four criteria described in a separate paragraph.
options.C: A JSON object with vendor names as keys, preserving the data for potential future import.
options.D: A side-by-side bullet structure with each criterion repeated under each vendor entry.

items.question:
A clinical operations coordinator uses Claude to draft patient discharge instruction letters. After the first draft the tone is too clinical. After a second-turn revision the reading level improves, but critical medication instructions are now missing. The coordinator is preparing a third iteration.

What is the BEST approach for the third iteration?

options.A: Start a fresh conversation so that prior instructions do not contaminate the new attempt.
options.B: In the same conversation, give one instruction that preserves what worked and restores what was lost: "Keep the plain-language tone from the last revision and reinstate all medication instructions from the original list."
options.C: Switch to Opus for deeper reasoning about clinical content.
options.D: Separate tone and content into two different prompts and merge the outputs manually.

items.question:
A legal operations manager uses the Claude API to generate contract risk summaries. Every response opens with "This contract presents several standard risks..." — a preamble she wants replaced by a direct numbered list starting with the highest-severity risk. She cannot modify the contract text or the system prompt.

Which technique addresses this MOST precisely?

options.A: Increase the temperature parameter so Claude generates more varied opening structures.
options.B: Add a negative instruction to the user message: "Do not begin with a preamble sentence."
options.C: Prefill the assistant turn with "1." so Claude continues directly into the first numbered item.
options.D: Append "Begin your response with the highest-severity risk" to the existing user message.

items.question:
An actuarial analyst is conducting a complex reserving model review with Claude in a single long conversation. After 25 exchanges, Claude's suggestions begin contradicting guidance it gave in turns 3 and 7. The analyst is unsure why this inconsistency is appearing.

What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.A: Claude actively discards earlier turns once a token threshold is passed, replacing them with an auto-generated summary.
options.B: Frequent turns degrade Claude's analytical capability on complex numerical topics.
options.C: The analyst's recent prompts introduced new constraints that directly overrode the earlier guidance.
options.D: In a very long conversation, attention to early turns diminishes as the context window fills, making it harder for Claude to stay consistent with guidance stated far back in the thread.

items.question:
A bid manager at a professional services firm sets a Claude Project instruction: "Always respond in formal British English; never use American spellings." In a subsequent chat within the same project, she writes: "Write this section in a casual, friendly tone — we're targeting a US technology audience." Claude responds formally throughout, using British spellings.

Which statement BEST explains this behaviour?

options.A: Project-level instructions take precedence over per-chat prompts when they directly conflict, so the project's formality and spelling rules override the chat-level request.
options.B: Claude cannot apply different tones to different outputs within a single project and requires a separate project per audience.
options.C: The chat prompt was ambiguous — "casual, friendly" did not explicitly override the formality rule, so Claude defaulted to the project setting.
options.D: This is a bug; per-chat prompts should always override project instructions when they directly contradict them.

items.question:
A training coordinator at a retail chain asks Claude to simplify a complex HR policy document for frontline staff. Her prompt reads: "Don't make it too formal, don't use legal language, and don't keep it long." The response is still overly formal and dense.

Which reframing is MOST likely to improve the result?

options.A: Add "Please" and "Thank you" to soften the tone of the request.
options.B: Replace the negative constraints with positive instructions: "Write at a 7th-grade reading level using short sentences and plain vocabulary, in bullet points. Target: a store associate with no HR background."
options.C: Specify the output format as a numbered list, which forces plain language.
options.D: Split the task into two prompts: one to simplify, then a second to shorten.

items.question:
A marketing operations manager at a B2B SaaS company generates personalised outreach emails for 80 prospects weekly. Each email requires the prospect's name, company, and a mapped industry pain point. She currently copies a base prompt and manually edits it per prospect — about 4 minutes each.

What would MOST effectively reduce this effort while maintaining quality?

options.A: Switch from Claude.ai chat to the API so email generation runs automatically without any prompt input.
options.B: Ask Claude to write a script that auto-populates prospect details from a spreadsheet.
options.C: Create a reusable prompt template with placeholders — {{prospect_name}}, {{company}}, {{industry_pain_point}} — and a batch workflow that substitutes real values for each row.
options.D: Upload all past successful emails to a Project knowledge base so Claude learns the pattern.

items.question:
A financial services analyst using Claude to draft a 40-section RFP response finds that the reply ends mid-sentence partway through section 22. The content produced so far is accurate and she wants to resume from the exact cut-off point without repeating work.

What is the BEST immediate action?

options.A: Start a new conversation and re-run the full prompt.
options.B: Send a follow-up message: "Please continue from where you left off, starting with the remainder of section 22."
options.C: Increase the max-tokens parameter so future responses are not cut off.
options.D: Ask Claude to summarise what it wrote and then regenerate the full document from the summary.

items.question: An internal auditor is producing a 30-section audit report. Each section must contain a finding statement, a risk rating, and a recommendation. Her first Claude run produces sections with inconsistent structure — some have risk ratings, others omit them; recommendations appear in different positions. What format specification would MOST reliably enforce consistency across all 30 sections?

options.A: "Use a standard audit report format throughout."
options.B: "Add clear headings to each section and ensure all sections are consistent."
options.C:
"Structure each section as follows:
**Finding [N]: [Title]**
Finding: [one sentence]

A pharma regulatory writer needs each module summary to be brief. Her first draft has eight sentences averaging 45 words each — far too long for the submission template. She wants to ensure the next run produces a tight, scannable summary.

Which specification would BEST control the output?

options.A: "Write a brief module summary."

items.question: A legal operations team has two distinct needs: (1) every contract review must apply the same five-category risk taxonomy and output format; (2) individual lawyers need to vary the depth and focus of each review based on deal type. What is the BEST configuration?

options.B: Create a separate Project for each lawyer so each can configure their own taxonomy independently.

items.question:
A content writer uses Claude.ai (not the API) and wants Claude to stop opening every response with "Certainly! I'd be happy to help with that." She has no API access and cannot modify system prompts programmatically.

items.question:
A senior partner at a consulting firm sets a Project instruction: "Always produce output a board-level executive could read in under 5 minutes." A junior analyst then writes a per-chat prompt asking Claude to "provide a fully detailed walkthrough of all 12 financial model assumptions." The output is neither concise enough for the executive nor detailed enough for the analyst.

Which explanation is MOST accurate?

options.A: The per-chat prompt overwrote the project instruction, causing Claude to produce a detailed output that was then automatically shortened.
options.B: Claude detected an explicit formatting conflict and applied a predefined conflict-resolution rule.
options.C: The project instruction imposed a hard token cap equivalent to a 5-minute read, which Claude truncated the detailed walkthrough to match.
options.D: The two instructions created an implicit conflict — executive brevity versus full technical depth — and Claude produced a compromise that satisfied neither goal.

An L&D manager has been working with Claude for 18 turns designing a training curriculum. Early turns established learning objectives; recent turns have produced module outlines that no longer reference those objectives. She wants to restore alignment without discarding the module work.

What is the BEST approach?

options.A: Ask Claude to produce a consolidated summary of the agreed objectives and current module outlines; use that summary as the opening context of a fresh conversation.
options.B: Scroll back to turn 3 and resend the learning objectives as a new message in the current thread.
